name: Colin Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have a music degree and have played trombone for twenty-six years. I do paid pit shows, teach four brass pupils and record short play-along parts for the youth band. The best part is hearing a pupil land a steady low note; the hard part is finding enough paid calls between productions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that mean at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner works variable hours as a care aide, and our children are grown. We rent and have three weeks of expenses saved; my pay is low for an experienced player, and there are few other groups close enough for a regular shift. I keep a paper diary and have never used AI.

say: I'd welcome **quicker notices** with correct rehearsal times and written pay.
I'd remind the crew that a **brass line** needs a player breathing with the singers.
think: A **closed show** could leave rent short even if AI changes little.
Our **three-week reserve** and variable partner hours make each call important.
do: Request **four paid pit calls** and written cancellation terms this week; keep four existing pupils.
Save **twenty** from an extra cleared show after rent, food and bus fares; continue using the paper diary.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary gaps between paid shows.
S0.quote: The computer is a small matter beside a missing paid Saturday.
fieldNote: His **thin cushion** and low pay make cancelled shows a rent problem before any major AI shift.
He **never uses AI** and keeps a paper diary by preference.

steps.text: Request four paid pit calls and written cancellation terms; keep four brass pupils
Save twenty from cleared extra show fee after rent, food and bus fares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the pit crew a quicker notice is useful only if it gives us the right rehearsal time and written pay. My brass line still comes from a person breathing with the singers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with AI mostly hype, a show can close and leave us short of rent. Three weeks saved and my partner's variable shifts make the next contract matter more than a new diary tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the producer to put the next four paid pit calls and cancellation terms in writing, and keep the four pupils I already teach. In the first year of this mild change I'll still use my paper diary and set aside twenty from a cleared extra show fee only after rent, food and bus fares are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the gaps between shows, even in this mild picture. The computer is a small matter beside a missing paid Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a show was cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter a matinee was cancelled and we were paid nothing because the call sheet had no cancellation term. I had to borrow the bus fare from my partner's food envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your children cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our grown children have their own bills. I won't count a family transfer as my weekly wage.

say: I'd ask whether **paid play-along orders** will be replaced.
I'd bring **fee sheets** to the association before accepting lower recording rates.
think: Recordings provide **one third** of my own pay and may shrink.
Three **weeks saved** cannot cover a term of missing invoices.
do: Bring **six invoices** and proposed rates to the musicians association this month.
Keep **paid calls** and pupils while seeking preparation/cancellation terms; require a paid approved demo before any AI trial.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic cut to my recording income.
S1.quote: Six invoices show what the work actually took, including the second take.
fieldNote: His **collective action** uses actual invoices rather than an assumed new job.
He remains **slow to adopt AI** and will not test with learner audio or unpaid instruction.

steps.text: Bring six recording invoices and proposed rates to musicians association
Keep paid pit calls and pupils; seek written preparation and cancellation terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the youth-band office whether its new software will replace paid play-along orders. I would take our fee sheets to the musicians association before anyone signs a cheaper recording rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those recordings make about a third of my own pay, and orders could shrink. I have three weeks of savings, so I cannot wait through a term of missing invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare six recording invoices with the youth band's proposed rates and take them to the association. In the first year of change I'll keep pit calls and pupils, ask the office for paid preparation and cancellation terms, and use no new AI tool until the band shows a paid, approved demonstration on its own non-pupil music.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because a third of my pay is exposed. The fee sheets give us something to bargain with, though they cannot create an order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the software on a pupil's part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't upload a pupil's playing to anyone's tool. The office can demonstrate with music it owns, on approved storage, and pay the instructor's hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a minimum paid recording and editing fee. Six invoices show what the work actually took, including the second take.

say: I'd warn that **2028 thinking AGI** reaches tracks before 2031 playing robots.
I'd ask for **signed live calls** while the producer still books players.
think: I expect **one-third pay** from play-alongs to end in 2028.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot carry that loss for long.
do: List **show and recording pay**, request signed calls and actual pension statements before stopping work.
Ask the **association** about paid replacement hours after 2028.
Seek **posted school work** if degree/experience qualify, written net after bus replaces lost fees and route works; keep music until signed offer.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected one-third pay loss against rent and thin savings.
S2.quote: I cannot treat turning 60 as a wage or decide to retire on a guess.
fieldNote: Expected **2028 recording loss** precedes 2031 trombone-playing robots and threatens a third of his pay.
A job move needs **posted eligibility**, written replacement net pay, workable transport and signed offer.

steps.text: List recording/show income; request signed producer calls and actual pension statements before stopping work
Ask association about paid replacement hours after 2028
Seek posted school job if degree/experience qualify, written net after bus replaces losses and route works
Keep pit shows and pupils until suitable signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the youth band that thinking AGI by 2028 can make play-along parts before robots play trombone around 2031. I would ask the producer for signed live calls while they are still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the play-along orders to end in 2028, taking about a third of my pay. Pit shows might survive until the playing robots arrive, but our three-week reserve will not absorb that first loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list recording and show income, ask the producer for signed paid calls and request actual pension statements before considering a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028 I'll ask the association about paid replacement hours and seek a posted school music-assistant job only if it accepts my music degree and teaching experience, written net pay after bus costs replaces lost fees and the route works; I'll keep pit shows and pupils until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about a likely loss of a third of my pay with rent due and almost no reserve. I can ask for a real vacancy, but I cannot make one appear nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the band offered replacement hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the youth band has not offered a different paid role. The association can ask about hours, but I will budget only a signed call or offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen a pension statement. I cannot treat turning 60 as a wage or decide to retire on a guess.

say: I'd price a **live brass circle** at the community hall before inviting anyone.
I'd require **signed room terms** before offering places.
think: My paid recordings may fade **before 2031** under ordinary software.
Our **rent account** cannot fund an empty class.
do: Offer **four-week brass circle** only after signed room/insurance/storage and eight fees covering room, cleaning, mouthpieces, my teaching/preparation and bus.
Inspect **loan horns**; defer and refund everyone if enrollment or instrument safety fails.
Renew **after 2031** only with eight fees paying room/cleaning/mouthpieces/own teaching/preparation/bus, signed terms and safe horns; keep booked pit calls/pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** until real deposits cover every class cost.
S3.quote: A brass circle with empty chairs is another unpaid shift, not a new wage.
fieldNote: His **experienced teaching** supports beginner brass instruction without inventing an advanced certificate.
The **eight-person floor** pays his preparation and transport, with full refund if safe places fail.

steps.text: Start brass circle: signed room/insurance/storage, eight fees cover room/cleaning/mouthpieces/own-teaching/preparation/bus
Inspect loan horns; defer and refund whole group if enrollment or instrument safety fails
Renew after 2031 with eight fees covering room/cleaning/mouthpieces/own-teaching/preparation/bus; signed terms and safe horns remain
Keep booked pit calls and current pupils while testing separate class

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the community hall that five years to AGI by 2031 lets me price a live brass circle, but no one gets invited until room terms are signed. Robots that play instruments follow around 2034, so paid teaching may matter sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recordings could end by 2031, and ordinary software might cut orders earlier. I know how to teach a beginner's first notes, but I cannot risk rent on an empty hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next autumn I'll propose a separate four-week beginner brass circle only after the hall signs room, insurance and storage terms. Eight adults must prepay enough for hire, cleaning and safe mouthpieces, my teaching, preparation and bus fares; the hall technician must inspect loan horns before fees are kept. In the first year after 2031 I'll renew only with the same eight-person paid floor, room agreement and safe instruments; if enrollment or safety fails I'll defer and refund the whole group, while keeping booked pit calls and current pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about filling eight paid places while recording orders may fade. A brass circle with empty chairs is another unpaid shift, not a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a loan horn is unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose slide or dirty shared mouthpiece stops a place being sold. If fewer than eight safe horns are ready and learners cannot bring their own, I return every deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for your preparation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The eight fees must pay my preparation and the bus as well as the room. I won't ask my partner to fund a class that only looks busy.

say: I'd get **written figures** for pay and pensions before changing work.
I'd ask for **current paid calls** before planning around 2039 robots.
think: At **68**, I may still need show and pupil income.
Three **weeks saved** do not prove that retirement will pay rent.
do: Request **actual pension statements** and written calls; save ten percent of cleared extra show fees after essentials toward two months.
Keep **paid shows and pupils** after 2036 while booked and until a suitable signed replacement offer.
Seek **posted community work** if recording/show fees both fall and pension gap remains; degree/experience accepted, written replacement net after travel, workable bus.
feel: I feel **anxious** about prolonged low pay and unverified retirement income.
S4.quote: A date on a pension letter will matter more to our rent than a guess from another player.
fieldNote: His **two-month reserve goal** depends on actual extra cleared fees after essential costs.
A **part-time job** remains conditional on posted hours, qualification, net pay, transport and a signed offer.

steps.text: Request actual pension statements and written paid theatre calls
Save 10% of cleared extra show fees after rent, food and bus costs toward two months
Keep paid shows and pupils after 2036 until suitable signed replacement offer
Seek degree/teaching-qualified posted job if recordings/shows both fall and pension gaps remain; written replacement travel-net, bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre that ten years to AGI by 2036 is time to get the pay and retirement figures in writing. Trombone-playing robots may follow around 2039, but I need this year's call sheet first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might still need shows and lessons; neither my music degree nor a birthday guarantees a pension amount. We have three weeks saved now, and a decade of uncertain calls does not fill that account by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request our actual pension statements and written paid calls, then save ten percent of any extra cleared theatre fee after rent, food and bus costs toward two months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid shows and pupils while booked; if recording and show fees fall and pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted part-time community music job only if my degree and teaching experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces the loss and the bus runs, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a long stretch of low pay, even with time to prepare. A date on a pension letter will matter more to our rent than a guess from another player.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra fee clears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No extra theatre fee means no transfer from that source. I won't move rent money into savings to make the target look better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a community job open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The local centre posted a helper job years ago, not now. I will apply only if a paid vacancy with real hours is open and I meet its requirements.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because play-along orders could end before I replace a third of my pay. Signed live calls, actual pension figures, association help and a posted qualifying job with written net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how many shows pay a player when the hall is dark. My trombone case can sit ready for weeks without earning a coin.

headlineQuote: My trombone case can sit ready for weeks without earning a coin.
portrait: Colin is a **58-year-old experienced trombonist** with a music degree, partner and grown children.
His **low pay**, three-week reserve and few nearby groups make ordinary contract gaps hard to carry.
He **never uses AI** and takes actual recording invoices to the musicians association as software cuts fees.
He tests a **separate brass circle** only with signed room terms, eight paid places and safe instruments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a third of Colin's income from play-along recordings.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed live calls**, actual pension figures, association action and a posted qualifying job with written replacement net pay would help.
